signals.excerpt:
Introducing GPT-6.1 Terra | OpenAI
# GPT-6.1 Terra
## Delivering fast and capable computer use at scale
We’re introducing **GPT-6.1 Terra**, a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos.
Terra continues to advance the cost-intelligence frontier across our model families, providing a new balance of speed, capability, and cost. Its standard API prices are 50% lower than those of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, making it practical for developers to automate high-volume work, like reading incoming invoices and entering their details into accounting software. In ChatGPT Work and Codex, your plan goes further with GPT-6.1 Terra—the same usage allowance covers more tasks than with GPT‑5.6 Terra and substantially more than with GPT‑6.1 Sol or GPT‑6 Astra.
## From visual understanding to action
We measured GPT-6.1 Terra’s computer-use capabilities on **Agents’ Last Exam,** a benchmark of professional tasks that includes turning architectural drawings into a 3D model and reviewing an animated film shot by shot to create a time-coded log for a restoration team. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra scores 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra at about one-third the cost. It even performs on par with GPT-6 Astra at only one-tenth its price per token. At max effort, Terra is over three times as token efficient as Claude Opus 5.5, and one-fourth its price per token, resulting in a \~9x lower cost per task. Terra is also much quicker, completing tasks **over three times faster** than both GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.
On **MMMU-Pro**, a benchmark of visual reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra outperforms GPT-5.6 Terra at every reasoning setting. It even nearly matches the scores of our most capable frontier model, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6.1 Sol at much lower cost.
**OSWorld 2.1** tests how well AI agents use desktop apps to complete multistep tasks, such as building a 3D model from a technical drawing. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-5.6 Terra’s best score at a fraction of the cost per task.
## A significant step up on factuality and coding
This year, we’ve invested heavily in reducing hallucinations and factual errors produced by our models. On our internal benchmark of error-inducing prompts, the error rate at low reasoning effort fell from 53.6% with GPT-5.6 Terra to 16.7% with GPT-6.1 Terra, a drop of nearly 37 percentage points. At maximum effort, the error rate fell by 18 percentage points to 4.3%, nearly matching the rates for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.
GPT-6.1 Terra marks a substantial improvement over GPT-5.6 Terra for software engineering. **Terminal-Bench 4.0** tests how well coding agents solve problems from the command line, such as fixing a webpage whose layout shifts as it loads. At maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6.1 Terra solves 50.3% of tasks, more than double GPT‑5.6 Terra’s published score of 21.5%. For the most complex coding tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra remain the better choice.
**Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1** tests how well agents use code to carry out scientific research tasks, such as tracking cell divisions in a time-lapse video. At max reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-6.1 Sol at lower cost, coming within five points of Opus 5.5 at less than one-fifth the estimated cost.
## Safety and alignment
As we make powerful AI more efficient and accessible, we continue training, testing, and refining our safeguards. GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra.
GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user’s task. More detail is available in the system card⁠(opens in a new window).
## Pricing and availability
Starting today, GPT-6.1 Terra is available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Developers can also access it through the OpenAI API as `gpt-6.1-terra`.
Standard API pricing is $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens, and $5 per million output tokens.

signals.title: Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK | Artificial Intelligence
signals.excerpt:
# Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK

by Prabhakar Chandrasekaran and Siddhant Sahu on 26 OCT 2026 in Advanced (300), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Technical How-to Permalink Share

This post builds enterprise agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). To see why that’s worth building, it helps to start with where ordinary Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) breaks down. Most RAG systems start the same way: they embed the question, fetch the nearest chunks from one index, hand them to a model, and return the answer. One retrieval, one generation. For a large class of questions that’s the right design, and there’s no reason to build anything more complicated.

It fails in a recognizable way. Ask a question whose answer spans two corpora, and a single retrieval returns half of what the model needs, which is worse than returning nothing, because the answer comes back fluent and incomplete. Ask a question where the right source depends on the question, and a single index has no mechanism to choose. Ask a question that needs a second look at the corpus after seeing the first result, and there is nowhere for that second look to happen.

Enterprise agentic retrieval answers all three by putting a reasoning agent in the loop. The agent decides whether to retrieve, which knowledge base to consult, and whether to go back for more before it composes an answer. This is the direction Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases have evolved. With the launch of the Managed Knowledge Base, retrieval is no longer a single embed-and-fetch call. It has become an agentic capability: multi-turn planning, tool-driven retrieval, and grounded, cited answers. The AgenticRetrieveStream API offers this as a first-class service feature rather than something you assemble yourself. That works, and it also introduces a genuinely harder operational problem. A single-shot pipeline is a function you can reason about by reading it. An agent that reasons and retrieves in a loop takes a different path on every question. By default you can see neither the path it took nor whether the answer it produced was any good. Observability stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the only way to know the system works.

...

In August 2024, Build an end-to-end RAG solution using Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock and the AWS CDK deployed the single-shot design as a CDK application: an Amazon Simple

...

### From RAG to enterprise agentic retrieval

Classic Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) does one retrieval and one generation. Enterprise agentic retrieval puts a reasoning agent in the loop: it decides whether and what to retrieve, can retrieve several times to refine, chooses which knowledge base is relevant (semantic routing), and only then composes a grounded answer with citations. With the Managed Knowledge Base, this is a first-class service capability, the AgenticRetrieveStream API performs the multi-turn planning, executes the retrieval, and returns a cited answer, rather than an orchestration layer you build and maintain over a raw vector search. That produces better answers on complex questions, but it also produces a more complex system to operate, which is exactly why observability and evaluation are built in from the start.

...

Step 0 — one-time, at deploy. Before any question is asked, each corpus in Amazon S3 is ingested into its own Managed Knowledge Base: Amazon Bedrock parses, chunks, embeds, and indexes it automatically. This happens once when the stacks deploy, it isn’t part of the per-question path, so it is drawn as a dashed arrow and marked step 0. Every question then follows steps 1–6:

1. A user sends a question to the agent hosted on the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The Runtime auto-instruments the whole reason-and-act loop with OpenTelemetry (OTEL) spans, so the system is observable from the very first call.
2. The agent’s reasoning model plans and routes across knowledge bases. Because each knowledge base is exposed as its own retrieval tool, the agent selects the tool whose topic matches the question, financial or weather, rather than searching one blended index.
3. The selected tool call is brokered by the AgentCore Gateway over MCP, authorized by the agent’s IAM task role and signed with SigV4, which invokes that knowledge base’s AgenticRetrieveStream API on the Managed Knowledge Base.
4. AgenticRetrieveStream does the within-knowledge-base work: it decomposes the question into sub-queries, retrieves iteratively from the data store that Amazon Bedrock manages (ingested from the corpora in Amazon S3), and synthesizes a grounded, cited answer that streams back through the Gateway.
5. The agent checks whether the returned context is sufficient. If not, it loops, routing and retrieving again, before composing its final answer. If so, it returns the cited answer to the user.

signals.title: 3 Ways to Boost MoE Inference on NVIDIA DGX Spark | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
Generating tokens faster starts with identifying what limits inference performance. In the batch-size-1 evaluation of Ling-3.0-flash from Inclusion AI on NVIDIA DGX Spark, profiling showed that decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out—the mixture-of-experts (MoE) computation and the output-layer projection that produces scores across the model’s vocabulary.

Those findings pointed to two ways to improve performance: reduce the weight traffic in each decode step and generate more tokens per verification round. This post examines three techniques that address those costs:

- Humming MXFP4 MoE kernels to improve execution of the routed-expert computation.
- Online FP8 quantization of the output layer, or LM head, to reduce its weight-read volume.
- Multi-token prediction (MTP) speculative decoding with NEXTN to draft and verify multiple tokens together.

This post explains how each optimization works, measures its effect, and examines an integration issue that can make the combined configuration slower than the baseline. Ling-3.0-flash serves as the

...

## Optimization 2: Online FP8 LM head quantization

In the checkpoint, the LM head is stored in BF16 and listed in modules_to_not_convert, so it is not quantized during loading. Its vocabulary GEMM is 157,184 × 2,560, and the entire weight block must be read for each generated token. Under a bandwidth bottleneck, it is therefore a high-value target for compression.

The optimization applies a dynamic FP8 quantization configuration only when constructing the LM head. The rest of the model continues to load with the checkpoint’s FP8/MXFP4 configuration. Moving the LM-head weights from BF16 to FP8 halves the read volume for this layer. The configuration is enabled with SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_LM_HEAD=1.

This setting is mutually exclusive with the baseline –enable-fp32-lm-head option, which outputs logits in FP32 and uses a slower vocabulary-GEMM path.

| Configuration | TPOT | Decode throughput | Relative to baseline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | 27.71 ms | 36.09 tok/s | — |
| + Humming MoE backend | 25.35 ms | 39.45 tok/s | +9.3% |
| + Online FP8 LM head | 22.76 ms | 43.94 tok/s | +21.7% |

Table 2. Cumulative effects of Humming and online FP8 LM-head quantization on NVIDIA DGX Spark, using a synthetic workload with 32K input tokens, 2K output tokens, and batch size 1. Adding FP8 increases decode throughput by 11.4% over Humming

signals.title: antoinezambelli/forge
signals.excerpt:
# forge

PyPI
Tests
codecov
Python 3.12+
License: MIT

A reliability layer for self-hosted LLM tool-calling. You give forge a set of tools; the model calls whichever it wants in whatever order. Workflow structure is opt-in — `required_steps`, `prerequisites`, and `terminal_tool` let you constrain the loop when you need to, but forge's guardrails (rescue parsing, retry nudges, response validation) apply with zero required steps too.

Forge takes an 8B local model from single digits to 84% across forge's 26-scenario v0.7.0 eval suite — and even lifts Sonnet 4.6 from 85% to 98% on the same workload (Anthropic numbers measured in v0.6.0; not re-run in v0.7.0 since the cost is non-trivial).

**What forge isn't:**
- **Not an agent orchestrator.** Forge sits inside one agentic loop and makes its tool calls reliable. Multi-agent graphs, DAG planners, and cross-agent coordination are out of scope.
- **Not a coding harness.** Forge is domain-agnostic. If you're building a coding agent (or already using one like opencode, aider, Cline), proxy mode lifts your existing harness with forge's guardrails — no rewrite.

**Three ways to use it:**

- **Proxy server** — Drop-in proxy (`forge-proxy` from the standalone distribution, or `python -m forge.proxy` from the Python package) speaking both the OpenAI chat-completions and Anthropic Messages (`/v1/messages`) APIs, sitting between any client and a local model server. Point OpenAI-compatible tools (opencode, Continue, aider) **or Claude Code** at it and forge applies guardrails transparently — the client thinks it's talking to a smarter model. Most popular entry point.

- **WorkflowRunner** — Define tools, pick a backend, run structured agent loops. Forge manages the full lifecycle: system prompts, tool execution, context compaction, and guardrails. **SlotWorker** adds priority-queued access to a shared inference slot with auto-preemption — for multi-agent architectures where specialist workflows share a GPU slot. Best when you're building on forge directly.

- **Guardrails middleware** — Use forge's reliability stack (composable middleware) inside your own orchestration loop. You control the loop; forge validates responses, rescues malformed tool calls, and enforces required steps.

Supports generic OpenAI-compatible endpoints, Ollama, llama-server (llama.cpp),
Llamafile, vLLM, and Anthropic as backends.

signals.title: Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs | Scientific Reports
signals.excerpt:
Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs | Scientific Reports
* Article
* Open access
* Published: 26 October 2026
# Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs
* Enmiao Feng 1,
* Gaike Wang 2,
* Pengfei Li 1,
* Yinuo Wang ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0004-3927-0742 3 &
* …
* Shan Huang 4
## Abstract
Large language model (LLM) inference workloads are bursty, have output lengths that are unknown at arrival, expose two resource-distinct phases (prefill and decode), and serve requests carrying heterogeneous service-level objectives (SLOs) on time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT). Prevailing schedulers rely on static heuristics that cannot adapt to this uncertainty, while online reinforcement learning (RL) is unsafe and sample-inefficient in production. We present URSA, an uncertainty-aware, risk-sensitive scheduler trained *entirely offline*, without interacting with a live serving system, on scheduling transitions generated by replaying historical request traces under existing heuristic schedulers. URSA (i) predicts a calibrated *distribution* over each request’s output length and derived key–value (KV) cache footprint rather than a point estimate; (ii) encodes the joint state of the waiting queue, heterogeneous GPU instances, and KV occupancy as a request–instance heterogeneous graph processed by a graph neural network; (iii) learns a dispatch policy with conservative, distributional offline RL whose reward jointly optimizes SLO attainment, goodput, and KV-overflow risk; and (iv) reserves memory at a class-dependent high quantile of the predicted footprint to bound out-of-memory events. Across the BurstGPT, Azure LLM inference, and Alibaba GPU-cluster traces, URSA raises overall SLO attainment from \\(71.3\\%\\) (FCFS) and \\(84.1\\%\\) (learning-to-rank) to \\(90.4\\%\\), cuts P99 TTFT by up to \\(3.3\\times \\), and reduces recompute/eviction events below \\(1\\%\\), approaching an oracle that knows true lengths. We analyze limitations, robustness to prediction error, and transfer to other scheduling domains.

signals.title: Tsinghua AI Open-Sources AKV, a Cache Engineering Server for LLM Agents on SGLang - MarkTechPost
signals.excerpt:
# Tsinghua AI Open-Sources AKV, a Cache Engineering Server for LLM Agents on SGLang

By

Asif Razzaq

October 26, 2026

Tsinghua University and CUHK researchers open-sourced AKV, a serving system for KV cache engineering in LLM agents. Instead of summarizing old history, agents drop selected KV cache entries and keep reusing the rest. Across 3 models and 4 agent benchmarks, average cost falls 27.7%. Average task score rises 1.7 points. The code is Apache-2.0 licensed and builds on SGLang.

...

## What does the AKV API look like?

The interface is stateless and OpenAI-compatible. Clients send the full message history and two optional fields. `drop_message` maps a trigger message index to the messages to drop. `reposition` lists the indices after which positions get compacted.

A `CachePolicy` builds those fields from a trigger, a selector and a reposition rule. Built-in policies are turn-based, token-based or model-based. A `CacheTool` lets the model call `drop_context` itself.

signals.excerpt:

# Hugging Face Publishes 207 WebGPU Kernels for Browser AI

Hugging Face has released 207 versioned WebGPU kernels, a JavaScript loader and Fleet benchmarking for local browser AI workloads.

Published

October 25, 2026

On this page More than a folder of shaders

- More than a folder of shaders
- Faster on an Apple M4, with caveats
- Fleet takes testing beyond one GPU

Hugging Face has released (opens in a new tab) an initial collection of 207 open-source WebGPU kernels for local AI workloads, accompanied by a JavaScript library that downloads and runs them directly from the Hugging Face Hub. Announced by Nico Martin (opens in a new tab) and Joshua Lochner (opens in a new tab), the collection covers the low-level operations that browser inference runtimes repeatedly need: matrix multiplication, normalization, convolution, attention primitives, quantization, broadcasting and tensor layout transformations. Everything is Apache 2.0 licensed. This is foundational work rather than another model demo. Faster browser inference ultimately depends on faster individual operations, and WebGPU portability alone does not guarantee good performance across every device.

...

## Faster on an Apple M4, with caveats

Hugging Face compared its kernels against ORT WebGPU on an Apple M4 GPU using a development version of ONNX Runtime Web 1.30.0. The evaluation started with 1,756 cases across all 207 operations. Hugging Face’s published aggregate covers the 809 cases where both systems produced matching outputs and reliable timings. Across those cases, the company reports a 2.57x geometric-mean speedup and a 1.90x median speedup, with 629 wins, 176 losses and four ties. Familiar operations showed more moderate improvements: Add reached 3.52x, Softmax 2.11x, LayerNormalization 2.22x and MatMul 1.14x. Some specialized workloads produced extreme results. A bilinear `Einsum` case ran more than 10,000 times faster, while a row-wise `CumSum` reported a 301x improvement.

# AWS open-sources Infinity, a Rust agent runtime that fits about 75,000 idle AI agents in 8 GB

2 days ago 10 min read

Updated: 19 hours ago

Expand image

Amazon Web Services has released Infinity, an open-source Rust runtime designed to let very large numbers of AI agents wait on slow tools without holding processes, threads or network connections while they wait. The project was introduced on October 23, 2026 on the AWS Open Source Blog by Shadaj Laddad, research lead for the Hydro team at AWS, and is published under the Apache 2.0 license as part of the Hydro project, a collaboration between AWS and the Sky Computing Lab at UC Berkeley. AWS describes the release as an early research prototype rather than a managed service, and it is asking developers for feedback on the design.

...

Infinity ships with three connected pieces: the runtime itself, a tool protocol called the Reactive Agent Protocol (RAP), and a coding agent called Infinity Code that is built on the runtime. The same agent code is meant to run either as a resident process on a laptop or as a stateless, event-driven deployment on AWS Lambda, for which the repository includes AWS CDK constructs.

signals.excerpt:
Liquid AI

# Introducing LFM3: Every Modality for Specialized Intelligence

OCT 27, 2026

Today, we’re excited to announce LFM3, our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) built for specialized intelligence. The LFM3 model family is multimodal by nature and brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one new shared backbone. The first release of the LFM3 family covers models in the 2B parameter range.

Built on a new hybrid architecture and 22T tokens of pre-training, LFM3 is far more expressive than LFM2 while maintaining its efficiency. The extra capacity in a small, fast model makes LFM3 the ideal starting point in its class for specialized intelligence: this is because it can be fine-tuned locally, it can run on any device, and it is capable enough to become a reliable expert on a specialized task.

The base and post-trained models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face, our Playground, and the Liquid AI API. Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune them locally.

## Highlights

- More capability per parameter: a new tri-hybrid architecture and training recipe allow LFM3-1.7B to outperform our previous LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters.
- Every modality, one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base. 
- Built for the edge: the text model fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit precision. 
- New flagship in-house vision and audio encoders.
- 256K context window for the text model.
- Made to be specialized: every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU.

LFM3 instances are ideal candidates for specialized intelligence. Fine-tune them on your own data, and deploy them where your application runs. Enjoy the article.

# Tensormesh Launches Tensormesh Platform to Cut LLM Inference Costs by Reusing KV Cache at Enterprise Scale

## Optimizing enterprise AI inference through intelligent multi-tier KV cache management

 This is a Press Release edited by StorageNewsletter.com on October 26, 2026 at 2:00 pm 

Tensormesh, creators of LMCache, an open-source KV caching technology, announced Tensormesh Platform, the data management layer for AI inference. This multi-tier, scalable KV cache management software deploys across infrastructure with an enterprise Kubernetes deployment. With intelligent, AI-native data at its core, Tensormesh Platform enables enterprises to optimize the efficiency, cost, and quality of every inference they run. This marks the arrival of the first enterprise-ready KV cache management offering that works with any LLM, inference orchestration software, and storage vendor.

...

Enterprises deploying Tensormesh Platform also benefit from:

- Tiered Caching: KV Cache is managed across HBM, CPU, and storage layers automatically
- Prefix Caching: reuses the computed KV cache for the opening part of a prompt
- NonPrefix Caching (CacheBlend): reuses computed blocks anywhere in the prompt, not just at the start, making Tensormesh Platform ideal for RAG
- Peer-to-peer KV transfer: fetches KV cache directly from any peer in the fleet
- Advanced cache controls: allows users to pin, look up, move, compress, and clear entries via controller APIs, per workload or fleet-wide

signals.title: 11,840 TPS on a single GPU
signals.excerpt:
11,840 TPS on a single GPU
# 11,840 TPS on a single GPU
#### Ara Khan
27 Oct 2026 — 4 min read
NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on October 15, and we reached **11,840 aggregate output tokens/sec** on one GB300 with **256 concurrent requests**. This blog post is a walkthrough of all the tricks we used to get there.
For context, this model is specifically designed to be a really fast, locally hosted model that can perform reasonably well across domains like document intelligence, coding, financial accounting, etc.
For the cluster of models in the same category, it turns out to be much, much faster than the others. And the benefit of having such a small, fast model is that you can post train it for special use cases.
At Cline, we are especially excited about easy to host open weight models, and we try to get the best inference config for fast and highly concurrent inference. Much like our work on AI Evals, we find that there are tons of nuances in inference engineering around choosing the particular thing you want to optimize for.
Thanks to our collaboration with the NVIDIA team, we got to play with an NVIDIA DGX Station and we wanted to maximize the model throughput on it. This GPU has a very powerful config for a single machine with a 252 GB GPU memory budget.
Starting out with the base config of vLLM `0.32.0rc1.dev190+g3f1bcfd82`, which took **67 GB** of memory, we were already getting **6,058 aggregate tokens per second** on a test of 512 input/output tokens with 256 concurrent streams. It's interesting to note that even the base config of the model is VERY strong and already tuned for high throughput inference.
Here are a few tricks we applied to raise the throughput(See Code here):
### 1. MTP Decoding
The very first trick we applied was the standard one, which is the MTP decoding head that came packed with the model. This is the simplest optimization, and it can be done a few different ways, so we tried MTP3, which got us to roughly **7,000 tokens per second**. We used the OMP1 config because single threading is more convenient here, as multiple threads lead to coordination overhead.
### 2. Async Scheduling
When scaling to multiple concurrent outputs, especially in a case like ours, the GPU does a lot of kernel work, but the CPU does a lot of scheduling work. So by using asynchronous scheduling, you aren’t blocked all the time while the GPU is processing.
### 3. Switching the Mamba kernel back to FlashInfer
This model supports both KV cache and Mamba backend layers.
Attention layers use KV cache and Mamba layers use recurrent state and short convolution history. In this use case, since we just wanted to hill climb on throughput, we tried the FlashInfer kernel, which gave us a jump to **7,800 tokens per second**. Again, it's not really clear to us why this worked but it worked as one of the large set of experiments we threw at the GPU. It's plausible that for certain GPU config this doesn’t work and that’s okay.
### 4. Switching the lookahead from MTP 3 to MTP 1
This one seems counterintuitive, as you would think that if more draft tokens are predicted, then throughput would increase, but sadly, that’s not the case. We don’t just need to predict tokens; we need to verify them, and if the verification fails, we waste model time. Since the GPU already has plenty of useful work to do at 256 concurrent threads, the extra overhead actually isn’t worth it.
This actually raised our throughput to **9.5K** with MTP 1.
### 5. Switching Mamba state to FP16 from FP32
The final step was an add on to Step 3, where we switched the Mamba state to FP16 with stochastic rounding. This, of course, led to a drop in precision and, consequently, a potential drop in evals, but since the goal here was to maximize throughput, it was well worth it.
## Conclusion
We learned a few things from this experiment that we sort of already knew. The first is that **inference engineering is extremely contextual**, and your capacity to scale very much depends on the traffic shape you are getting. We used a few tricks here, like using MTP 1 instead of MTP 3, or switching the Mamba kernel to FlashInfer, that worked perfectly well to give us the throughput rise, but they could have just as easily hurt the throughput in other sorts of load tests. Also, using a trick like FP16 could potentially lower the eval score.
**In general we recommend that people figure out the best traffic shape and do inference for that traffic shape alone.**
We have a few long term predictions:
1. People will be able to self host and run dozens of parallel local agentic threads. Here, see this video of 32 parallel Clines running Nemotron 3.5 Super VL seamlessly on a single DGX Station (this is a real video with no speedup).
1. It will be cheaper to run a set of self hosted models compared to paying for inference. In this case the napkin math of API usage vs. a fully occupied GPU led to us getting a 66% discount on inference. This means that it's cheaper for you to use our inference recipe and pay for a GPU rather than hit a model router and pay per API call provided you are fully utilizing the GPU.
2. Autoscaling models will be like a self healing task where agents will figure out the best possible config for a given traffic shape. Imagine if an agent had full access to Grafana metrics; then the agent could automagically run load tests on a held out GPU (one that doesn’t affect the real traffic), iteratively figure out the best possible config for any traffic coming to a certain endpoint, and then safely autoscale and migrate the traffic to the new configuration. This way, we could have self healing autoscale configs for inference endpoints that automagically understand their own role and optimize costs and scale to just the right amount of GPU usage as a function of time. Since agents are very good at end to end testing in a loop and monitoring a careful migration we believe that **the future of Inference engineering autoscaling is Agentic**.

signals.excerpt:
Published October 27, 2026 

# Introducing Governor, a context-driven model router for coding agents 

 

#### Table of Contents 

Agentic coding has taken off, and token use has skyrocketed with it. Much of that spend goes to finding things in your code rather than writing it. In our measurements, 60% to 80% of what a coding agent costs goes to searching and reading its way around your codebase, and nearly all of it is billed at frontier-model prices. 

Today we are launching Governor, a context-driven model router for coding agents. Governor is one layer between your coding agents and your models, and your team keeps using Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Pi, or GitHub Copilot exactly as they are. 

A router, on its own, cuts the price of a token. Governor also replaces the grepping and searching your agents do, and the two savings stack. It routes each request to the best model and reasoning level, and it grounds every request in your code through Bito’s code context engine. 

For an engineering team, that means the same coding tasks ship for half to a third of the cost, and faster. In one customer’s A/B test on their own engineering tasks, cost per task dropped 48% and task success held at 100%.

...

## How Governor works 

Coding agents let you change what models you access, so now you just point your base URL at Governor to auto-route across models. Governor speaks the Anthropic and OpenAI APIs, runs in or alongside your existing gateway on your own provider keys, and serves the same code context to every developer server-side.

signals.title: Cerebras Explains Trillion-Parameter Model Deployment | PithWire
signals.excerpt:
# Cerebras Explains Trillion-Parameter Model Deployment

Original: Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models

## Why This Matters

Shows a viable path to serving trillion-parameter open models at commercial inference speeds.

 PithWire Take The math is clean—but 59 wafers per model deployment is a steep hardware ante for most buyers. 

Cerebras published a technical breakdown of how it deploys multi-trillion-parameter models across WSE-3T wafers, using Kimi K3's ~3T parameters as the example, achieving 1,000–2,000+ tokens per second.

Cerebras detailed its approach to running frontier-scale models across clusters of WSE-3T wafer-scale chips, each carrying 44 GB of on-chip SRAM. Using Kimi K3—an open-source 3-trillion-parameter model with 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers—as a worked example, the post walks through how the company fits weights into memory and pipelines inference.

With 4-bit quantization, Kimi K3's full weight payload is roughly 1.5 TB. Each of its 93 layers occupies about 16 GB. Dense layers, which require KV cache storage proportional to active requests, get one layer per wafer. Linear-attention layers carry a fixed-size state regardless of context length, so two fit per wafer. That arithmetic yields 59 wafers total for the full model.

Weights stay fixed in place on each wafer. Only activations move between wafers via RDMA over Ethernet, with roughly 2-microsecond hops. Cerebras frames the setup as an assembly line: each wafer is a pipeline stage, and tokens travel through sequentially. The company claims this architecture supports 1,000–2,000+ tokens per second at scale.

Kimi K3 itself scores 88.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 91.2% on BrowseComp, edging GPT-5.6 Sol on the latter benchmark.

In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation, it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Use it to draft proposals, interpret technical drawings, investigate codebases, and build agents that operate across business systems. Established AWS controls help you secure workloads, govern access, and audit model invocation activity. 

You can get started in the Amazon Bedrock console or programmatically through supported Amazon Bedrock APIs. For information about supported AWS Regions, endpoints, APIs, features, inference profiles and pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation.

signals.title: Native Opens SQLite Preview With 40× Token Claim | Zeniteq
signals.excerpt:
# Native Opens SQLite Preview With 40× Token Claim

Native’s open research preview puts Markdown context behind SQL, with promising vendor benchmarks that readers can test against their own agent workloads.

AI News 9 min read Published Oct 28, 2026 · 8:40 AM PHT

Jim Clyde Monge

Native has released a research preview of a context-engineering architecture that offloads retrieval tasks from AI agents to a SQLite database. By structuring Markdown documents into relational tables, agents can execute recursive SQL queries to traverse links and filter records rather than repeatedly scanning raw text. This approach significantly reduces context window usage and latency, with Native reporting 40 times fewer tokens and six times faster response times compared to standard Markdown-grep baselines. These efficiency gains are most effective for relationship-heavy queries, such as tracing project dependencies or approval chains, rather than general document summarization.

...

Native describes the release as a research preview for a context-engineering architecture. Markdown remains the familiar source material, while SQLite provides a structured way for agents to retrieve relevant information.

The research post connects this work to Native’s broader goal of “context sovereignty”: keeping working knowledge accessible and usable independently of a particular AI provider. The company says its core engine is already open source, with more planned after the preview.

The product itself remains an early-access offering. Native’s homepage asks readers to join a list and advertises one-line setup once admitted. Access to source code and immediate access to the packaged product are therefore separate things. (Native homepage)
